corrections.anchor_text: “If your work̨s deserve statues, your conduct deserves chains,” wrote Frederick the Great to Voltaire. Voltaire replied: “I demand justice and death.” This came at the end of a friendship between the two that had attracted the attention of the civilized world. Voltaire had been invited to live with Frederick at the latter's court. For a while they got along well together, but their eccentricities, the differences in their personalities, inevitably led to trouble. They quarreled and parted. The break came about in a rather unusual way. Frederick had given Voltaire permission to have published in the royal printing office a Defense of Lord Bolingbroke. Voltaire was accused of slipping in an additional work, “The Diatribe of Dr. Akakia.” The latter was a merciless onslaught on Maupertuis, the President of the Royal Academy of Berlin, and Frederick's very close friend. corrections.anchor_text: A young man, only twenty-three years of age, who had conquered more than half of the civilized world, was sitting in his tent reading a letter. The message was from Darius, the great king of the rich Persian dominions, whose army Alexander had practically destroyed a while before on the plains of Issus. Darius had managed to get together a remnant of his followers and did not stop running until he crossed the Euphrates. Then he organized another great army, larger than that of his pursuer. In this message he was admonishing the upstart from Macedonia for overrunning his kingdom. He did not even address Alexander as king. But fear of further conquest prompted him to offer Alexander half of his realm, with the Euphrates as a boundary, if he would return to Greece. General Parmenio, a wise old counsellor who had followed Phillip, Alexander's father, was urging the young king to accept the proffered terms of peace. Parmenio warned him of the great Persian fleet in his rear, of revolt and other dangers, if he advanced. Alexander spent his life in grand robbery, Diogenes in vagabondage; the richest and the poorest; or might it not be reversed? Alexander thought that the greatest virtues were glory and splendor. Diogenes believed that to gain virtue one must avoid all physical pleasure.

corrections.anchor_text: It has been said that the greatness of a man is determined by the influences for good that he sets in motion. Beginning his work for a religious sect when a greater part of the world was against him, losing his family, friends, and even his reputation, yet by his undying love for a cause, by the strength of his intellect and the force of his will, St. Paul commanded a hearing, caused thrones to bow before his influence and lifted the Cross of Jesus above the Roman Eagle. We can see how a man will go forth in a blaze of glory and give his life for his country. But here is a man who picked up the thread of a religion, and it so appealed to him that he wanted to give his life for others as part payment for the great joy which had come to him. He died daily for mankind through his sufferings. It is all very strange to some of us. At three different times he was flogged with Roman rods. Once he was stoned almost to death. Three times he was shipwrecked, and for a whole day and night floated upon the face of the deep. On three different occasions he looked death in the face without wincing: once when the mob was about to kill him in the Temple; once when his ship was wrecked on the Mediter-ranean, and again when he sat in the prison in Rome wait-
corrections.note: Retype italicized editorial narrative block p0051-b0003 from body to editorial.

Bok noticed the large number of requests which came to Longfellow for his autograph. Sometimes more than a dozen would come in one mail. Longfellow would take a card out of a drawer and write his name on it. “There are a good many of these every day,” said the great poet, “but I always like to do this little favor. corrections.anchor_text: Not all princesses are the dream creatures which children read about in story books. Not all of them are courted by a handsome prince wearing a glorious uniform, with trappings and plumes. Not all princesses are as beautiful as a goddess nor as good as angels. Many of them live very real lives, suffer the pangs of disappointed love, pass dreary days waiting for news of the battle-front, or go into mourning for the loss of loved ones. A modern princess who was greatly beloved by the people of her country, was Princess Alice of England, the daughter of Queen Victoria. She seemed to possess all of the qualities which every princess should have. When Queen Victoria's husband, Prince Albert, died, the Queen's grief was unbounded. It was a tragedy which seriously threatened the normal course of her life. During these dark days it was the faithfulness of the young princess which attracted the attention of the English people and called forth a beautiful tribute to her from the London Times. Princess Alice was tender-hearted, charitable, courageous, energetic, religious. She was happily married to Prince Louis of Hesse.
